title: Mapping the Fire–Ecosystem–People Nexus in a Southern African Mosaic: Explainable Fire-Regime Typologies and Stewardship Zones for Eswatini, 2001–2025
content: Fire in African savannas and mosaic landscapes is often reduced to burned-area totals or treated as a simple hazard. This framing is too narrow for landscapes where fire is simultaneously an ecological process, a livelihood practice and a governance concern. We developed an event-based fire-regime and fire-stewardship framework for Eswatini, a topographically compressed southern African country with protected areas, communal rangelands, cropland margins, plantation landscapes and peri-urban interfaces. Global Fire Atlas-derived fire-event histories were organised by fire year and intersected with approximately 10 km2 hexagonal units for 2001–2025. We quantified burned-area rate, fire-event frequency, recurrence, seasonality, large-fire dominance, pyrodiversity and trends, and then classified observed fire-regime types independently from socio-ecological predictors. Socio-ecological drivers were interpreted with XGBoost regression and exact TreeSHAP diagnostics. Fire activity was sharply seasonal: July–September accounted for 78.2% of burned area, with August alone contributing 34.2%. Eight fire-regime types were identified, ranging from low-information and episodic-fire units to frequent small-fire mosaics, large-fire-dominated areas and emerging burned-area intensification regimes. The explainable model showed strong held-out performance for burned-area rate (R2 = 0.71; Spearman rho = 0.75) and identified human modification, goat density, elevation, forest probability, fuelwood dependence and precipitation seasonality as leading but non-linear drivers. Translating these diagnostics produced six adaptive fire-management zones that separate protected-area stewardship, conservation-sensitive fire management, settlement–livelihood interfaces, late-season risk reduction, monitoring areas and integrated landscape fire management. The framework is designed for Eswatini, but its logic is directly transferable to African countries where fire policy must move beyond blanket suppression towards place-based stewardship.
